title: The books between (Wisdom 3:1–3)
hookLine: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include Wisdom, Sirach and others; Protestants often call them Apocrypha

cards: Put three Bibles side by side on a table: one from a Catholic parish, one from a Greek Orthodox church, one from a Baptist church down the street. They all begin with Genesis and end with Revelation.
But count the books, and the counts don't match. The Protestant Bible has sixty-six. The Catholic Bible has seventy-three.

Orthodox Bibles have a few more again. Same faith in Christ, same Gospels, different shelves. It comes down to a handful of books from the centuries just before Jesus, and what each church calls them.

teach.b: They include Tobit, Judith, the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Baruch, and First and Second Maccabees, plus extra passages in Esther and Daniel.
Most were written, or survive, in Greek, in the Greek Old Testament many early Christians read. Catholics call them deuterocanonical: deutero means second, canon means the measuring rule, the list.

Second-listed, not second-rate: their place on the list was settled later, after some debate. The Council of Trent confirmed them for Catholics in 1546. Orthodox churches also read them, and include a few others.
In the Reformation, Martin Luther gathered these books into their own section between the testaments: not equal to scripture, he said, but useful and good to read.
Many Protestants call them the Apocrypha, from a Greek word for hidden.

teach.h: TRENT, LUTHER, AND THE KING JAMES.
teach.b: The 1611 King James Bible itself printed them between the testaments, and Anglicans still read from them in worship.
So: Catholics and Orthodox Christians hold them as scripture. Many Protestants honor them as edifying history and wisdom, but not as scripture. Now a taste of one.
The Wisdom of Solomon, written in Greek, speaks of good people who die young or unjustly.

teach.h: THE SOULS OF THE RIGHTEOUS ARE IN THE HAND OF GOD.
teach.b: In the King James Apocrypha: "But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and there shall no torment touch them." To the foolish, it goes on, they seemed to die, but they are in peace.
It's read at funerals across traditions: whatever shelf you keep it on, people have held this line at gravesides for a very long time.

how: Catholic and Orthodox Christians read the deuterocanonical books in worship, and Wisdom 3:1–9 is a common reading at Catholic funerals; Anglican and Episcopal churches read from the Apocrypha in their lectionaries, while many other Protestant churches read them privately, if at all.

games.q: you're Martin Luther, translating the Bible into German. these books are in the Bible you know, but you doubt they're scripture. what do you do?
o: print them in their own section, as useful and good to read.
leave them exactly where they were.
games.why: Luther gathered them between the testaments, as books not equal to scripture but useful and good to read. the King James Bible followed a similar pattern.

practice: Let the line come back slowly, word by word: the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God.
Then bring to mind someone who has died, a grandparent, a friend, someone you never got to say goodbye to, and picture them held, not lost.
If you pray, you can entrust them to God with the line itself; if you don't, just sit with them a moment in that picture of an open hand.

wordCard.voice: Deuterocanon. The second-listed books, like Wisdom and Sirach: scripture for Catholics and the Orthodox, the Apocrypha for many Protestants.
